title: Dynamic Causal Graphs Under Parametric Uncertainty
one_liner: Instead of learning a fixed causal diagram, learn how the causal connections change as the system's operating conditions shift.
lead: Real industrial systems do not have fixed causal relationships. A chemical reactor's temperature affects the reaction rate differently at high pressures than low pressures. Standard causal discovery methods assume the graph is static, missing these shifts. This paper proposes a new framework where each causal link is not a single number but a function that changes with measurable system settings (like pressure, time, temperature), using Polynomial Chaos Expansions to keep the math tractable.

problem.h2: Fixed causal graphs miss how relationships evolve
paras: Causal discovery is the task of learning which variables influence which other variables by looking at real-world data. Standard methods learn a fixed causal graph: X causes Y with strength 2.5, and that is the whole story.

But real systems change their causal behavior based on operating conditions. In a chemical reactor, increasing the reactor pressure shifts how temperature affects the reaction rate. In a power grid, demand elasticity changes with time of day. A naive causal graph treats the system like a machine with permanent wiring, when the actual wiring is reconfigurable.

When causal links vary, a static graph becomes misleading. You learn a causal diagram that is true on average but false in any specific operating regime, useless for predicting what will happen when you change one variable in a real scenario.

callout.html: Causal relationships in real systems depend on operating conditions, but standard discovery methods assume the graph is frozen.

panels.title: 1. The usual causal graph
panels.viz_args: Temperature → Reaction Rate → Yield (all fixed numbers)
panels.caption: Standard methods learn one arrow strength per relationship.

panels.title: 2. The problem: same arrow, different effect
panels.caption: At low pressure, temperature barely moves yield; at high pressure, huge effect.

panels.title: 3. The paper's move: each arrow becomes a curve
panels.viz_args: Temperature → f(Pressure) → Reaction Rate (f adapts with pressure)
panels.caption: Replace each fixed number with a function that depends on system state.

panels.title: 4. Polynomial Chaos fits that curve
panels.caption: A polynomial in operating conditions approximates how influence changes.

panels.title: 5. Result: predictions adapt to actual conditions
panels.viz_args: Learned dynamic graph: 90.9% F1-score on chemical reactor
panels.caption: Dynamic model nearly doubles accuracy over static baselines.

steps.text: Record which operating conditions each observation occurred under.
Express each influence as a polynomial function of the measured conditions instead of a single fixed number.
Fit polynomials efficiently using orthogonal basis functions so the method scales to many operating conditions.
Learn which causal links exist and what their polynomial coefficients are from observational data.
Prove mathematically that the functional causal structure can be uniquely recovered from the data.

paras: The paper replaces each static causal weight with a function. Instead of learning 'Temperature affects Yield with strength 2.5', you learn 'Temperature affects Yield with strength that depends on Pressure'.

hidden.h2: Parametric causal structure: how influence shifts
hidden.name: dynamic causal link functions
paras: The hidden quantity is how each causal influence changes as operating conditions shift. Concretely, it is the set of polynomial coefficients describing Temperature's effect on Yield as a function of Pressure.

The paper estimates this by fitting Polynomial Chaos Expansions — orthogonal polynomial basis functions — to data, then solving a causal discovery problem in polynomial coefficient space to identify which links exist and what their functional forms are.

Effect of X on Y at mid param
Effect of X on Y at high param
heat.caption: Darker means stronger causal influence or more evidence for that polynomial.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is the influence that each variable exerts on others, but now this influence is not constant — it is a curve that depends on what operating conditions the system is in.

Polynomial Chaos Expansions represent each causal link as a sum of orthogonal polynomial basis functions in the operating-condition space, enabling tractable identification of the functional causal structure.

mechanism.h2: Why changing the causal links to functions fixes the problem
paras: When causal links are functions instead of fixed numbers, the model can capture how the same variable pushes differently under different conditions. If Temperature's effect on Yield is written as a polynomial in Pressure, the fitted polynomial will show a weak slope at low Pressure and a steep slope at high Pressure.

Polynomial Chaos Expansions are chosen because they provide an orthogonal basis — each polynomial term is independent, which means fitting one coefficient does not interfere with fitting others. This matters: if you tried to fit the full space of possible functions, the computation would explode exponentially, but orthogonal polynomials keep it manageable even when you have many operating conditions to account for.

The paper proves mathematically that under standard causal assumptions (no cycles, no unmeasured confounders), the functional causal structure is identifiable — meaning there is only one correct set of polynomial coefficients that fits the data and causal graph. This matters because when a solution is mathematically unique, the learning algorithm can safely search for it without worrying that multiple different solutions might fit the data equally well; uniqueness guarantees that finding a good fit means you have found the true causal structure.

On real chemical reactor data, these dynamic causal graphs double the prediction accuracy of static methods, because the model can now say 'in this operating regime, Temperature has a stronger influence', matching how the actual reactor behaves.

stages.s: Observational data tagged with operating conditions
Fit Polynomial Chaos Expansions to approximate each variable's dependence on operating conditions
Run causal discovery in polynomial coefficient space to find which links exist
Prove the discovered structure is uniquely identifiable from data
Dynamic causal graph: each link is now a function of operating conditions

math.h2: The core equation: functional causal links
math.words: Each causal link from variable X to variable Y is approximated as a polynomial in the parameter vector p. The link strength is not a single number but a sum of polynomial terms, where each term is an orthogonal polynomial basis function times a learned coefficient.
symbols: the strength of causality from X to Y when the system parameter is p
the learned coefficient for the k-th polynomial term
the k-th orthogonal polynomial basis function in parameter p
the measurable system operating parameter (e.g., pressure, temperature, time)

worked.title: Tiny worked example: Temperature effect on Yield
lines: Suppose Pressure is the operating parameter and we fit: f(Pressure) = 0.5 + 1.2 * Pressure + 0.3 * Pressure^2
Same Temperature change, but at 3 atm the influence is 3.4 times stronger than at 1 atm—the function captures the regime shift.

math.note: The polynomial coefficients are learned from data so the fitted function matches how the observed causal influence actually varies with system state.

charts.title: Static causal discovery (baseline)
charts.note: A fixed causal graph misses how reactor behavior changes with operating conditions.

charts.title: This paper (dynamic with Polynomial Chaos)
charts.note: Learning dynamic causal links as functions of reactor conditions nearly doubles accuracy by capturing how influences shift with different settings.

items.html: If the reactor's causal structure also depends on an operating condition you did not measure (e.g., catalyst aging), the polynomial fit will appear to have extra noise or systematic error, and identifiability breaks.

items.b: Too few observations in some regimes.
items.html: If all your data comes from one operating point, the polynomial coefficients cannot be learned—you need variation across different operating conditions to fit the curve.
If the true functional form is nonpolynomial (e.g., a sharp threshold), a low-degree polynomial will misfit. If the degree is too high, overfitting wastes data on noise.

items.b: Done right: measure key conditions and collect varied data.
items.html: If you identify which operating conditions matter, measure them consistently, and gather data across the full range of settings, the method recovers the true dynamic structure.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic chemical reactor simulation where one reaction pathway's yield depends on temperature when pressure is low, but depends on concentration when pressure is high. Generate observational data tagged with both pressure and temperature. Run standard static causal discovery and compare to learning dynamic causal links with Polynomial Chaos Expansions. The demo should make it clear that the static method learns an average causal graph that is neither fully true at low pressure nor high pressure, while the dynamic method recovers separate causal structures for each regime.
demo.metric_eq: F1-score = 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall) on correctly identifying dynamic causal links
demo.closing: The key metric to watch: a static graph will show moderate F1 at each regime (neither regime fits the global graph); the dynamic graph will show high F1 at every regime (the polynomial adapts to each).
